hero.title: Kolabr vs Notion
hero.lede: Notion is a blank canvas, and a good one. To run client work on it, somebody builds the portal, the tracker and the sharing, connects a chat tool and a video tool, then keeps all of it working. Kolabr is the finished room your client walks into: the conversation, requests with a clock, the wiki, calls and events, ready the day you open a channel.

owner.title: The tracker nobody has to own
owner.lede: A Notion setup belongs to whoever built it. When they move on, the knowledge of how it works goes with them. Kolabr’s structure is the product, so there is nothing to hand over.

points.title: Nothing to design
points.body: Nobody decides how your company models a client, a request or a deadline, and nobody documents that decision.

points.title: Nothing to repair
points.body: No property somebody renamed, no view somebody deleted, no automation that stopped when its builder left.

points.title: Every channel the same
points.body: Someone who knows one client channel knows them all, including a new starter in their first week.

cost.title: One subscription, or a stack
cost.lede: Per person the prices are close. What differs is everything else you pay for, because Notion has no chat and no calls.

scale.title: At Business level
scale.notion: Notion Business is $20* per member. SCIM provisioning and the audit log are kept for Enterprise, which is quoted.
scale.kolabr: SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning and an unlimited, exportable audit log are all included.

cost.note: * Yearly fees, per person per month. Billed monthly, Notion Plus is $12 and Business $24; Kolabr Pro is $10 and Business $25. Notion prices checked 6 October 2026.

items.title: Can Notion replace a chat tool?
items.body: No. Notion has comments on pages and blocks, but no chat between people and no calls, so client work in Notion runs beside a separate chat tool and a separate video tool. In Kolabr the conversation, the calls, the requests and the wiki are in the same channel, and your own team gets a Team channel that no guest can be added to.

items.title: Notion has forms. How does a client ask for something in Kolabr?
items.body: They say it in the channel. One step turns the message into a numbered request with a category, an owner and a response target, and routing sends it to the right person. The client then watches that request: who has it, its status and how long is left. A form gets the question in; a request keeps the promise in sight until it is kept.

items.title: Can I build a request tracker in Notion?
items.body: Yes, and people build good ones. The question is who keeps it working. A Notion tracker is a database somebody designed, with views somebody configured and automations somebody maintains, and it usually belongs to one person who eventually moves on. In Kolabr requests are part of the product: categories, owners, statuses, response targets and the channel’s dashboard exist the moment you create it.

items.title: Both offer free guests, so what is the difference?
items.body: What a guest joins. In Notion a guest is shared individual pages, to view, comment on or edit. In Kolabr a guest joins a channel: the conversation, their open requests and the clock on each, the wiki, calls and events for that relationship, all at once. You are not deciding page by page what a client may see.

items.title: Which is cheaper?
items.body: Per person the two are close: on yearly terms Notion Plus is $10 a member and Kolabr Pro is $8.50 a user. The difference is what else you pay for. Notion has no chat and no calls, so client work on it needs a chat tool and a video tool as well, and Kolabr Pro includes both. At Business level, Kolabr includes SCIM provisioning and a full audit log, which Notion keeps for its quoted Enterprise plan.

items.title: Can we use Kolabr and Notion together?
items.body: Plenty of teams do. Notion keeps the long-form internal knowledge it is already full of, and Kolabr runs client channels, where the conversation, the requests and the wiki for that relationship belong together. The channel wiki is for what a client or a new starter needs, not a company encyclopaedia.

proof.title: Proof takes one week
proof.lede: Pick one client and open a channel. There is nothing to model, no template to choose and no database to design first.

steps.text: Open the channel and invite the client. The conversation, the requests and the wiki are already in it; you set up none of the three.
The first requests have numbers, owners and dates, and you have written the two or three wiki articles that stop the same questions coming back.
You will know whether anything still needs building. That is the only test this page is asking you to run.

cta.title: Nothing to design. Start working.
cta.body: Free for one channel, no card. Seven days on Pro or Business when you want the rest. Open a channel for one client and see it working the same afternoon.
